title: ISRAEL WAS TOLD NOT TO TOUCH A WOMAN FOR THREE DAYS BEFORE MEETING GOD—WAS SEX REALLY THAT DIRTY?
paragraphs: ISRAEL WAS TOLD NOT TO TOUCH A WOMAN FOR THREE DAYS BEFORE MEETING GOD—WAS SEX REALLY THAT DIRTY?

One of the most misunderstood commands at Mount Sinai reveals something astonishing about marriage, holiness, the human body, and the God who does not despise what He created. But the deepest revelation is not about what Israel had to avoid for three days. It is about what Jesus Christ accomplished so that sinners could finally draw near to God.
There is a verse in the Bible that can make even faithful Christians uncomfortable.
Not because it is difficult to read.
But because of what it seems to suggest.

Imagine being a husband standing at the foot of Mount Sinai. You have watched God humiliate Pharaoh, divide the Red Sea, and deliver your family from generations of slavery. You have seen the cloud leading you through the wilderness. You have eaten bread that appeared on the ground.
And now, the God who rescued you is about to descend upon a mountain.
You are about to witness something terrifyingly holy.
But then Moses delivers an instruction that seems almost out of place.
Do not go near a woman for three days.
Wait.
What?
Was God saying that intimacy between a husband and wife was dirty?
Was the marriage bed somehow offensive to His holiness?
Did a man have to avoid his wife to become spiritually acceptable?
And if sexual intimacy was something God Himself designed, why would He command Israel to abstain from it before meeting Him?
These are not foolish questions.
They are the kinds of questions people sometimes carry silently because they are afraid that asking them will make them appear irreverent.
But Scripture does not need us to protect it from honest examination.
In fact, when we read this passage carefully, in its original language and biblical context, we discover something far more profound than a prohibition about sex.
We discover a distinction between what is sinful, what is ceremonially restricted, and what is holy.
And ultimately, we discover why Jesus Christ is the only reason any of us can approach a holy God with confidence.
But first, we need to return to the mountain.
Because something extraordinary was about to happen.
The Israelites had escaped Egypt, but Egypt had not entirely escaped their thinking.
For generations, they had lived under Pharaoh's authority. Their lives had been shaped by slavery, fear, humiliation, and the worship practices of a pagan empire.
Now they were free.
But freedom from slavery was only the beginning.
They needed to learn what it meant to belong to the living God.
And at Sinai, God was preparing to reveal Himself in a way that would forever shape Israel's understanding of holiness.
Exodus 19:10–11 records the Lord's instruction to Moses:

“Go unto the people, and sanctify them to day and to morrow, and let them wash their clothes, And be ready against the third day: for the third day the LORD will come down in the sight of all the people upon mount Sinai.” (KJV)
Notice what God commanded.
The people were to prepare themselves.
They were to consecrate themselves.
They were to wash their garments.
They were to be ready.
And then, in Exodus 19:15, Moses said:
“Be ready against the third day: come not at your wives.” (KJV)
The King James Version uses the expression “come not at your wives,” while many modern translations render the command along the lines of “do not go near a woman.”
The Hebrew text reads:
אַל־תִּגְּשׁוּ אֶל־אִשָּׁה
ʾal-tiggešû ʾel-ʾiššâ
A close rendering is:
“Do not approach a woman.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root נגשׁ (nāgaš), meaning to approach or draw near.
The noun אִשָּׁה (ʾiššâ) means “woman” and can also mean “wife,” depending on the context.
Here, the command is commonly understood as a temporary prohibition of sexual intercourse in preparation for the divine appearance.
The Hebrew does not explicitly say, “Sex is dirty.”
It does not say, “Women are spiritually inferior.”
It does not say, “Marriage is unholy.”
And it certainly does not establish that faithful husbands and wives must avoid marital intimacy whenever they want to pray or worship.
Those conclusions would go beyond what the passage actually teaches.
So why did God require this temporary abstinence?
To understand that, we must first recognize something that modern readers often overlook.
In the Old Testament, ceremonial uncleanness and moral sin were not identical categories.
That distinction changes everything.
Under the Mosaic Law, certain perfectly ordinary human experiences could produce temporary ritual impurity.
Childbirth involved periods of ritual purification.
Contact with a dead body could make someone ceremonially unclean.
Certain bodily discharges also resulted in temporary impurity.
And Leviticus 15:18 specifically states that when a man and woman have sexual intercourse involving an emission of semen, both are to bathe and remain ceremonially unclean until evening.
But here is the crucial detail.
The passage does not call lawful marital intercourse sinful.
It describes a temporary ritual condition.
That matters because something can be morally permissible while still being subject to ceremonial restrictions in a particular covenant setting.
Ritual impurity was part of Israel's system of worship and holiness. It regulated access to sacred spaces and participation in certain religious activities.
It did not automatically mean that someone had committed an evil act.
Think about childbirth.
God commanded humanity to be fruitful and multiply in Genesis 1:28.
Yet childbirth also involved ritual purification under Leviticus 12.
Would it make sense to conclude that giving birth was morally wicked?
Of course not.
The ritual category served a different purpose.
The same principle helps explain Exodus 19.
Israel was being prepared for an extraordinary encounter with God's manifest presence.
This was not an ordinary day.
It was not an ordinary gathering.
And it was not an ordinary mountain.
The temporary abstinence was part of a larger pattern of consecration.
The people were being taught to recognize that approaching the holy God was not something to treat casually.
But there is an even deeper truth here.
The God who instructed Israel to abstain temporarily from sexual relations is the same God who created human sexuality in the first place.
Before there was a serpent in the garden, before shame entered human experience, before sin corrupted relationships, God created man and woman.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
And Genesis 2:25 adds something beautiful:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” (KJV)
Read that again.
They were naked, and they were not ashamed.
Before the fall, there was no need to hide.
No fear of being exposed.
No exploitation.
No manipulation.
No sexual shame.
No broken trust.
Their nakedness existed within the goodness of God's creation.
And Genesis 1:31 declares that God saw everything He had made, and it was very good.
Marriage and its physical union were not embarrassing mistakes that God later regretted.
They belonged to His good design.
Sin did not create sex.
God created human beings as embodied creatures capable of marital union.
Sin corrupted human desires and relationships, but corruption of a gift does not make the gift itself evil.
A fire can warm a home.
The same fire, misused, can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The problem is what happens when it is taken outside its proper boundaries.
Likewise, Scripture treats sexual intimacy within marriage as good while condemning sexual immorality, exploitation, adultery, and other violations of God's design.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.” (KJV)
The contrast is unmistakable.
Marriage is to be honored.
Sexual sin is to be judged.
Those are not the same thing.
And that brings us to a painful reality.
Some people reading this article were taught to associate their bodies with shame long before they understood what the Bible actually says.
Perhaps you grew up hearing that every sexual feeling was filthy.
Perhaps you entered marriage carrying guilt you did not know how to explain.
Perhaps you were taught so much about avoiding sexual sin that nobody ever explained the goodness of marital intimacy.
Or perhaps your story is different.
Perhaps sexuality became a place of real sin, betrayal, addiction, exploitation, or heartbreak.
Perhaps someone crossed a boundary that should never have been crossed.
Perhaps you have spent years confusing what someone did to you with who you are.
And somewhere along the way, shame became louder than the truth.
Please hear this carefully.
The Bible's teaching on holiness is not permission for anyone to humiliate you, abuse you, or treat your body as worthless.
Your body matters to God.
Your choices matter to God.
Your wounds matter to God.
And the Gospel speaks to both human sin and human suffering without pretending they are the same thing.
If you have sinned, Christ calls you to repentance and offers forgiveness.
If you have been harmed, the evil committed against you is not your guilt to carry.
And if you have been taught that holiness means hating your body, you need to know that biblical holiness is not hatred of God's creation.
It is belonging to the God who created us.
But return with me to Sinai.
Because the mountain was about to tremble.
Exodus 19:16 describes thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet.
The people trembled.
Moses brought them out of the camp to meet God.
The mountain was covered in smoke because the Lord descended upon it in fire.
The smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace.
The mountain shook violently.
And the trumpet grew louder and louder.
Can you imagine standing there?
You had seen the sea open.
You had watched Egypt's power collapse.
But now the ground beneath your feet was shaking.
And the God who delivered you was revealing His holiness.
Suddenly, the instruction to wash garments, prepare for three days, and temporarily abstain from marital relations no longer seems like a random religious restriction.
It belongs to the seriousness of the moment.
Israel was being summoned into a covenant relationship with the Creator of heaven and earth.
And God was teaching them that His presence was not ordinary.
There were boundaries around the mountain.
Exodus 19:12 warned the people not to touch it.
The danger was not that the mountain itself was morally evil.
The danger was that God had designated it as the place of His holy manifestation and had established boundaries that Israel was forbidden to cross.
Holiness was not something human beings could redefine according to personal preference.
God Himself determined how His people were to approach Him.
And the lesson was not that wives were dangerous.
It was that Israel's encounter with God demanded consecration and obedience.
Notice another important detail.
The command in Exodus 19:15 was addressed to the people in a particular historical situation, as part of preparation for a particular event.
It was not presented as a universal three-day abstinence requirement for every believer before worship.
We must be careful not to turn a temporary command into a permanent law that Scripture itself does not establish.
This becomes even clearer when we turn to the New Testament.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3–5, the apostle Paul teaches that husbands and wives have mutual responsibilities within marriage.
He warns them not to deprive one another of marital intimacy except by mutual agreement, for a limited time, so they may devote themselves to prayer, and then to come together again.
This is astonishingly relevant to Exodus 19.
Paul recognizes that temporary abstinence may serve a legitimate spiritual purpose.
But he also insists that such abstinence within Christian marriage should be consensual and temporary.
He does not teach that sex contaminates prayer.
He does not teach that spouses become spiritually inferior through marital intimacy.
And he does not command Christians to abstain for three days before attending church, receiving Communion, or drawing near to God in prayer.
Instead, he treats marital intimacy as a legitimate part of married life.
A couple may voluntarily set it aside for a season of focused prayer.
But the act of setting aside something good for a special purpose does not make the good thing evil.
You may fast from food.
That does not make food sinful.
You may step away from ordinary work for worship.
That does not make honest work unholy.
And Israel's temporary abstinence at Sinai did not make marital intercourse dirty.
Consecration is not always about rejecting something evil. Sometimes it involves temporarily setting aside something good to give undivided attention to something sacred.
That is a lesson many of us desperately need.
Because we often misunderstand surrender.
We assume that if God asks us to give something up, He must hate it.
But sometimes the issue is not whether a thing is bad.
Sometimes the issue is whether we are willing to place even good things beneath the authority of God.
A career can be good.
Family can be good.
Marriage can be good.
Rest can be good.
Success can be good.
But none of those gifts should become greater than the Giver.
At Sinai, Israel was learning that the God who rescued them deserved their reverence, obedience, and undivided attention.
And that truth reaches far beyond marriage.
It reaches into our homes.
Our phones.
Our private habits.
Our ambitions.
Our relationships.
Our hidden compromises.
Our worship.
And the quiet places where we know God has been calling us to obey Him, but we keep finding reasons to delay.
Perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not whether sex was dirty at Sinai.
Perhaps it is this:
If God asked you to lay aside something you genuinely love so that you could obey Him, would you trust Him enough to do it?
Not because the thing itself was evil.
Not because your body was shameful.
But because He is God.
That question exposes something deeper than outward religion.
It reaches the heart.

And before we congratulate ourselves for being more enlightened than the Israelites standing beneath that terrifying mountain, we should remember that the human heart has not changed as much as we think.
We still struggle to surrender.
We still negotiate with obedience.
We still want God's blessings while resisting His authority.
We still prefer a God who comforts us over a God who also confronts us.
And sometimes, we would rather debate an ancient command than allow the living Word of God to examine our own lives.
But this is where the story becomes even more extraordinary.
Because Sinai was never the end of God's redemptive story.
It was pointing forward.
To another mountain.
To another covenant.
To another Mediator.
And ultimately, to Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 12:18–24 deliberately contrasts the terrifying experience at Sinai with the privileges believers have through the new covenant.
The writer reminds Christians that they have not come to the mountain associated with blazing fire, darkness, gloom, and tempest.
Instead, they have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the Mediator of a new covenant.
The contrast is breathtaking.
At Sinai, Israel was commanded to remain behind boundaries.
In Christ, believers are invited to draw near to God.
At Sinai, the people trembled before the divine manifestation.
Through Christ, redeemed sinners receive access to the Father.
But do not misunderstand the contrast.
God did not become less holy.
His righteousness did not diminish.
His judgment against sin did not disappear.
The difference is not that God lowered His standards.
The difference is that Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
At Sinai, the people were commanded to prepare.
At Calvary, Jesus gave Himself as the sacrifice through which His people are cleansed.
At Sinai, access was restricted.
Through Christ, the way into God's presence has been opened.
Hebrews 10:19–22 teaches that believers have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus and are called to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith.
And there is a Greek expression in Hebrews 10:22 that deserves our attention:
προσερχώμεθα
proserchōmetha
It means:
“Let us draw near.”
The verb comes from προσέρχομαι (proserchomai), meaning to approach or come near.
Here, it is an exhortation addressed to believers.
Think about the movement of the biblical story.
At Sinai, Israel was told not to cross the appointed boundary.
In Hebrews, believers are urged to draw near to God through Jesus Christ.
Not because human beings have become holy through their own efforts.
Not because sin has stopped mattering.
Not because ceremonial preparation has somehow been replaced by casual irreverence.
But because Jesus has provided the cleansing and access that His people need.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
And it is where the question about three days of abstinence becomes part of something much greater.
At Sinai, the people prepared for the third day because God was going to descend before them.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day, according to the Scriptures.
These are distinct events, and Exodus 19 does not explicitly identify its three-day preparation as a prophecy of Christ's resurrection.
We should not pretend it does.
But when we read the Bible as one unfolding account of God's redemption, we can recognize a profound contrast.
At Sinai, sinners prepared to witness God's holy presence under strict boundaries.
Through the death and resurrection of Christ, forgiven sinners are welcomed into fellowship with God through their Savior.
The connection is not a hidden numerical code.
It is the larger biblical movement from the old covenant to the new, from restricted access to the access secured by Jesus.
And that is more beautiful than any forced symbolism.
Because the greatest problem facing humanity was never the goodness of marital intimacy.
It was sin.
Our rebellion.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our deceit.
Our selfishness.
Our attempts to become our own authority.
Our habit of hiding what God already sees.
And no amount of external preparation could erase that guilt.
You could wash your garments a thousand times.
You could abstain from every earthly pleasure.
You could memorize religious rules.
You could appear respectable in front of everyone who knows you.
But none of those things could purchase forgiveness for your sins.
Only Jesus Christ can save.
The Son of God lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for sinners.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message about behaving better.
It is the announcement of what God has done through His Son to redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
And perhaps this is where the article stops being about ancient Israel.
Perhaps this is where it becomes about you.
Because some of us are still standing at the foot of a mountain we have built out of our own shame.
We believe God is holy.
We believe Jesus died for sinners.
We believe forgiveness is possible.
But somewhere deep inside, we wonder whether forgiveness is really possible for someone with our history.
Someone who knew better.
Someone who crossed boundaries.
Someone who betrayed trust.
Someone who returned to the same sin after promising never to do it again.
Someone who carries memories that still make them lower their eyes when they pray.
And when we hear the words “Do not come near,” something inside us whispers:
That sounds like what God must be saying to me.
But if you are hearing that whisper, listen carefully to what the Gospel actually declares.
Jesus did not come to congratulate people who had already made themselves righteous.
He came to save sinners.
He did not shed His blood because human beings were capable of washing themselves clean.
He shed His blood because we needed a Savior.
And He did not rise from the dead merely to give us another set of religious instructions.
He rose as the victorious Lord, through whom repentance, forgiveness, and new life are proclaimed.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
It teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
It leads us into repentance.
It transforms our desires.
It gives us a new identity in Christ.
And it reminds us that our worst chapter does not have to be the final chapter of our lives.
Maybe you were unfaithful.
Maybe you have been trapped in pornography.
Maybe your marriage is wounded by years of secrecy.
Maybe you have used religion to hide a double life.
Maybe you have been wounded by someone else's sin and have confused their wrongdoing with your worth.
Maybe you are exhausted from trying to appear holy while feeling spiritually empty.
Whatever your story, do not confuse God's call to repentance with a declaration that redemption is impossible.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Stop defending what He calls sin.
Stop carrying guilt He calls you to surrender.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Seek wise and trustworthy help where healing and accountability are needed.
And remember that transformation is not achieved by pretending the past never happened.
It begins by bringing the truth into the light of Jesus Christ.
John 8 records the account of a woman accused of adultery.
In that account, Jesus exposes the hypocrisy of her accusers and tells the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)

There is an important textual note here: the account in John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and modern Bible editions often mark its textual status. Its familiar portrayal of mercy joined with a call to holiness is consistent with teachings found elsewhere in the New Testament.
And the words traditionally associated with this account capture a truth we must never separate.
Mercy does not require us to pretend sin is good.
And holiness does not require us to deny that forgiveness is real.
Jesus Christ calls sinners to repentance.
And Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
That is the difference between condemnation that leaves a person in despair and Gospel conviction that leads a person toward repentance and life.
So no, Exodus 19:15 does not teach that sex within marriage is inherently dirty.
It does not teach that women are spiritually contaminating.
It does not teach that God despises the human body.
It teaches, within its historical setting, that Israel was commanded to consecrate itself for an extraordinary encounter with the holy God.
Its temporary abstinence instruction belongs to that preparation.
And when we read it alongside Genesis, Leviticus, 1 Corinthians, Hebrews, and the larger story of redemption, we see a consistent biblical truth.
God's gifts are good.
God's holiness is real.
God's commands matter.
And God's grace in Jesus Christ is greater than the sin from which He came to save us.
But there is one more thing I do not want you to miss.
At Sinai, the people had to prepare for God's descent.
In the Gospel, the Son of God came into our world.
The eternal Word became flesh.
He entered human history.
He experienced hunger, weariness, sorrow, rejection, and suffering, yet without sin.
And He willingly went to the cross to accomplish our redemption.
The God whose holiness made the mountain tremble did not abandon His purpose to dwell with His people.
He fulfilled His saving promises through Jesus Christ.
The same biblical story that teaches us to fear the Lord also teaches us to trust His mercy.
And the Gospel does not end with sinners forever trembling at a distance.
It calls those who belong to Christ to draw near.
What a Savior.
What mercy.
What grace.
If this has exposed a place where you have confused shame with holiness, or where you have been resisting God's call to repentance, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.

And if you are fighting a private battle and need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.” You do not have to disclose intimate details publicly to be worthy of prayer, compassion, or Christian fellowship.
There may be someone reading the comments who needs to know that they are not the only person struggling to understand grace.
There may be a husband or wife who needs to hear that their marriage is not something God despises.
There may be a young believer who has mistaken bodily shame for biblical purity.
There may be someone carrying the consequences of sexual sin who needs to hear both the call to repentance and the promise of forgiveness through Christ.
And there may be someone who has never understood why Jesus came.
This is why I am asking you to do more than read this and move on.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass someone who misunderstands Scripture.
But because biblical truth can bring clarity where confusion has been allowed to grow.
Our desire is to keep bringing people back to Scripture, to the person and work of Jesus Christ, and to the truth that repentance and grace belong together.
But I also want to share something personal about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.

Producing careful biblical teaching, creating discipleship resources, and making Christian literature available to people who may never be able to afford an extensive theological library requires time, effort, and financial support.
And we believe that ministry support should be an invitation made openly, never a burden placed on someone's conscience.
We want those resources to keep reaching people.
We want to continue expanding the library.
We want to produce more Christ-centered books, more Scripture-based articles, and more resources that help people move beyond surface-level religion into serious biblical discipleship.
For those who choose to give, it can be a voluntary expression of Christian generosity and support for Gospel-centered work.
But I want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor cannot be bought.
And no monthly payment makes anyone more acceptable to Him.
Jesus Christ alone is our righteousness and our hope.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and they do not measure anyone's faith.
What matters most is that the Gospel continues to be proclaimed faithfully and that people continue growing in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
Read the Scriptures.
Pray for the ministry.
Share these teachings with others.
Invite someone to explore the free library.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
And sometimes one faithful act of sharing a biblical message can introduce someone to a truth they have never heard explained clearly.
Before you leave, though, I want you to remember the mountain.
Remember the smoke.
Remember the thunder.
Remember the trembling people who were told to prepare for the presence of the living God.
Remember that the command to abstain for three days was not a declaration that marriage was filthy.
It was part of a sacred moment of covenant preparation.
And then remember the cross.
Remember the Savior who shed His blood.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the One who calls us to holiness is also the One who provides forgiveness and new life through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not invite you to make peace with your sin.
It invites you to be reconciled to God.
It does not tell you to hate the body God created.
It calls you to honor Him with your body.
It does not promise that following Jesus will remove every earthly struggle.
It promises that those who belong to Him are no longer abandoned to the guilt and dominion of sin.
And it does not ask you to manufacture your own righteousness before approaching the Father.
It calls you to trust the righteousness and saving work of Jesus Christ.
So when someone asks you again:
“Why did God tell Israel not to go near a woman for three days before meeting Him?”
You can answer with confidence.
Because the holy God was preparing His covenant people for an extraordinary encounter with His presence.
Not because lawful marital intimacy was inherently sinful.
Not because women were unclean by nature.
Not because human bodies were mistakes.
But because consecration mattered, God's holiness mattered, and His people needed to learn reverence and obedience.
And now, through the finished work of Jesus Christ, believers are invited to draw near to that same holy God with reverence, gratitude, repentance, and faith.
That is not permission to treat holiness lightly.
It is the greatest reason to take holiness seriously.
Because the God who saves us by grace also calls us to walk in newness of life.
And the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners does not leave them unchanged.
At Sinai, the people trembled because God was coming near; at Calvary, the Savior suffered so that forgiven sinners could be brought near to God.
